catalog_quote: In the vast majority of Gaelic words, the word-initial syllable is stressed. Exceptions are generally borrowings, such as buntàta ... 'potatoes', and some adverbs, such as an-diugh 'today' ... and days of the week

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Nance & O Maolalaigh, JIPA Illustration 'Scottish Gaelic', section 'Tone, intonation and stress', PDF pp.11-12) is present verbatim in the copy we hold lines 614-652. The two StressTyp2 passages named in the domain locator (973 Dorian 1978:36; 975 Gillies 1993:164) are present as cited in the on-disk StressTyp2 SQL dump, and the held Gillies 2009 handbook chapter (p.249) independently states 'one stress occurs, falling on the initial syllable' with loanword exceptions (buntata, sineubhar, mailisidh). Note the record's top-level quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank -- the evidence sits in the domain quotation/sources; that is a bookkeeping gap, not a sourcing gap. (2) Deciding source: a 2021 peer-reviewed JIPA Illustration by the field's leading specialists, i.e. a modern primary phonetic description; nothing in Glotto

sources.quote: "In the vast majority of Gaelic words, the word-initial syllable is stressed. Words containing a svarabhakti vowel (see above) are unusual in terms of stress and it has been claimed that both vowels bear stress (Bosch & de Jong 1997)."
